I'm 73 now, been farming these same fields for 55 years. Only went to primary school, but I know my land better than any book. It's just me and the old woman — two of us, getting old, only four hands between us. We got 5 mu total. Not much, but it's ours, and I know every corner of it.

The wheat went in last October like always, 2 mu of it. I put down compound fertilizer then, about 100 jin per mu, same as my neighbor Lao Zhang. Now it's spring, and I need to topdress with urea when it greens up — maybe 30 jin per mu. I'll irrigate three more times: once now, once at jointing, once at grain filling. Every time I pump water I think about the electricity bill, but dry wheat means no bread. I'll spray twice for insects and once for weeds. If the weather holds I expect about 900 jin per mu, same as last year.

Cotton is our cash crop — I keep 3 mu in cotton. I've been doing cotton since the 1990s. I'll plant around April 20th, after the rotary tillage. Basal compound fertilizer, about 100 jin per mu. Cotton needs water at seedling, flowering, and boll stage — three times total. The real cost is pesticide. Bollworm is terrible lately, I spray almost every week during summer, maybe 13 or 14 times total. That's where the money goes. I'll hire some women from the village to help pick in autumn, pay them by the day. Last year I got about 500 jin per mu, I hope for the same.

After we cut the wheat in early June, I got less than one week to get the maize in. No time for deep tillage — maybe quick rotary or just plant into the stubble. I plant 2 mu of hybrid maize. Basal compound fertilizer, about 80 jin per mu. If the summer rains are good, maybe only irrigate once or twice. Two insecticide sprays, one herbicide. Maize is easier than cotton, less work on these old bones.

Money is tight. Compound fertilizer got expensive again. I can't afford to push everything to the maximum. I'd rather apply a bit more than too little — a bad year hurts worse than wasting a little fertilizer. The wheat and maize feed us and the chickens, cotton brings cash for medicine and daily needs. That's how we get by.
